papers_read.title_as_printed: Diagnosing Mild Cognitive Impairment Among Racially Diverse Older Adults: Comparison of Consensus, Actuarial, and Statistical Methods (Devlin et al., J Alzheimers Dis 2022; 85(2): 627-644; PMC author manuscript)
Data-driven classification of cognitively normal and mild cognitive impairment subtypes predicts progression in the NACC dataset (Edmonds et al., Alzheimer's Dement. 2024;20:3442-3454)

what_each_reports.P-955: 354 Penn ADRC participants (consensus NC or MCI at baseline; 68% White, 29% Black); 14 tests in 6 domains, z-scores from published norms adjusted for age, education, gender. MCI rates: consensus 44%, actuarial Jak/Bondi (>1 SD on 2 tests in a domain) 53%, 5-class latent class analysis on domain scores 41% (44% with race-adjusted norms). Consensus-LCA concordance 90% (kappa 0.80); actuarial-consensus kappa 0.68; actuarial-LCA 0.70. Consensus predicted outcomes best overall (dementia HR 29.33 vs actuarial 13.54 vs LCA 9.49).
what_each_reports.P-1084: 26,255 non-demented NACC UDS participants from 46 ADRCs; Ward hierarchical cluster analysis of UDS memory, attention, TMT and language z-scores derived from a 'robust CN' NACC subsample (n = 9742). Five clusters; cluster-derived MCI 58.8% of the sample vs consensus MCI 32.4% (plus 6.6% impaired-not-MCI). 84.2% of consensus MCI fell in cluster MCI groups; 44.5% of consensus 'normal cognition' fell in cluster MCI groups. Of progressors to dementia, 80.3% were cluster-MCI at baseline vs 68.2% consensus-MCI.

quantity_a: Share of a single-ADRC memory-centre sample (consensus NC/MCI, 44% consensus MCI) classified as MCI by a 5-class LCA on 6 domain z-scores using published demographic norms, relative to consensus.
quantity_b: Share of the multi-site NACC non-demented sample (32.4% consensus MCI) classified as MCI by Ward hierarchical clustering on UDS test z-scores normed on a 'robust CN' subsample, relative to consensus.
incompatible_if_same: No. A data-driven partition's MCI rate is a property of the specific procedure (algorithm, battery, normative reference, number of classes) and of the sample's case mix; 41% vs 44% in one frame and 58.8% vs 32.4% in another can both be true. P-1084's own discussion cites P-955's result (reference 23) and attributes the difference to robust-CN norms and single-ADRC vs NACC samples, presenting both findings as true.

gates.task: mismatch: T6 diagnostic-method comparison vs T2 progression (both also compare data-driven vs consensus classification).
gates.dataset_family: overlapping: both are NIA ADRC data using the NACC UDS; the Penn ADRC (P30 AG072979, PI David Wolk, a P-955 co-author) is listed among the NACC-contributing centres in P-1084, so P-955's participants are plausibly inside P-1084's sample.
gates.validation_tier: n/a: descriptive classification comparisons without a trained predictive model (counted as matched).

endpoint_and_metric: incompatible: different classification procedures (LCA with probabilistic classes on domain means vs Ward clustering on test z-scores), different normative references (published age/education/sex norms vs NACC robust-CN regression norms), different batteries (14 tests incl. CERAD vs UDS subset), and different base rates of consensus MCI (44% vs 32.4%).
independence: Not independent in data: Penn ADRC contributes to NACC (listed in P-1084's acknowledgments), and P-955 participants completed the NACC UDS. Authorship distinct; P-1084's senior author (Bondi) co-developed the actuarial criteria that P-955 evaluates.
grounds: The two MCI rates come from different data-driven procedures (5-class LCA on domain means with published norms vs Ward hierarchical clustering on test z-scores with robust-CN norms), so 'data-driven vs consensus' names two different quantities.

P-1084 explicitly discusses P-955's 90% concordance finding and attributes the difference to its robust normative sample and the larger multi-site frame, i.e. the authors present both results as true of their own procedures.
The sampling frames differ in consensus-MCI base rate (44% in P-955 vs 32.4% in P-1084) and P-1084 attributes its excess MCI to consensus diagnoses tracking CDR and requiring subjective complaints.
The dataset family overlaps (Penn ADRC contributes to NACC), so the pair also fails the independence requirement for a genuine contradiction.

evidence_quotes.quote: MCI rates by consensus, actuarial criteria, and LCA were 44%, 53%, and 41%, respectively.
Consensus and LCA diagnoses of MCI demonstrated substantial agreement, with concordant diagnoses for 90% of cases.
All participants completed the Uniform Data Set prescribed by the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center and additional cognitive tests.

Overall, the cluster analysis classified a greater number of individuals as having MCI (58.8% of the sample) than did the consensus method (32.4% of the sample with MCI, plus another 6.6% impaired-not-MCI).

The current finding of a discrepancy between the cluster-derived classifications and consensus diagnoses differs from a previous study23 that found 90% concordance between statistically-determined MCI diagnoses from a latent profile analysis and consensus diagnoses.
While both studies leveraged demographically-adjusted neuropsychological z scores, only the current study derived z scores from the performance of robust cognitively normal participants.
Cluster analysis of baseline neuropsychological data was conducted by entering z scores into a hierarchical cluster analysis using the Ward method

record_defects: claim_b and the conflict_statement say P-1084 supplies 'NO count' for its direction claim; the PDF gives 58.8% cluster-MCI vs 32.4% consensus-MCI (plus 6.6% impaired-not-MCI) and a full cross-tabulation (Table 2).
The record calls P-1084's method 'agnes' hierarchical clustering; the PDF states hierarchical cluster analysis using the Ward method and never names agnes.

The resolution_note Best_Metric string for P-955 ('actuarial-consensus 0.72, consensus-LCA 0.68') is wrong: primary kappas are consensus-LCA 0.80, actuarial-consensus 0.68, actuarial-LCA 0.70 (race-adjusted 0.79, 0.72, 0.75).

The record treats Penn-inside-NACC as structural inference; P-1084's acknowledgments list the Penn ADRC grant (P30 AG072979, PI David Wolk, a P-955 co-author) and P-955 states its participants completed the NACC UDS, so the overlap is documented, though exact participant overlap is not quantified.
The record omits that P-1084 itself cites P-955 and explains the difference (robust norms, single ADRC vs NACC), which is the key fact for the verdict.
P-1084 describes P-955's method as 'latent profile analysis'; P-955 used latent class analysis. Minor, in P-1084 not the record.
what_would_change_the_verdict: A study applying the same data-driven procedure and normative reference in two comparable samples and obtaining opposite departures from consensus; the two documents here use different procedures, norms and frames, and one cites and reconciles the other.
